outcome.candidate_text:
Assume for contradiction that \(x>1\). For every odd prime \(p\mid y\) with \(p\nmid x\), let \(\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\) be the multiplicative order of \(x\pmod p\), and let \(L\) be the least common multiple of these orders; take \(L=1\) if there are no such primes.

Choose an odd prime \(\ell\nmid x^{2L}+1\), and set
\[
k=\ell L,\qquad N=x^{2k}+1,
\]
and
\[
e=\begin{cases}2,&2\mid y\text{ and }x\text{ is odd},\\1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
\qquad Q=N/e.
\]
We claim that \(\gcd(Q,xy)=1\). Certainly \(\gcd(N,x)=1\). If an odd prime \(p\mid y\) also divides \(x\), then \(N\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(p\mid y\) but \(p\nmid x\), then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\mid L\), so
\[
x^{2k}=x^{2\ell L}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence \(N\equiv2\pmod p\). Thus no odd prime divisor of \(y\) divides \(N\). If \(x\) is even, then \(N\) is odd; if \(x\) is odd, then \(N\equiv2\pmod8\), so the definition of \(e\) removes the only possible common factor \(2\) with \(y\). Hence \(\gcd(Q,xy)=1\).

We next prove
\[
\operatorname{ord}_Q(x)=4k.
\]
Indeed, \(Q>2\), and \(x^{2k}\equiv-1\pmod Q\), so the order divides \(4k\) but does not divide \(2k\). If the order were a proper divisor \(d\) of \(4k\), then \(d<2k\). Consequently,
\[
0<x^d-1\le x^{2k-1}-1<\frac{x^{2k}+1}{2}\le Q,
\]
contradicting \(Q\mid x^d-1\). Thus the order is \(4k\).

By Fermat's congruence,
\[
N=x^{2\ell L}+1\equiv x^{2L}+1\not\equiv0\pmod\ell.
\]
Therefore \(\gcd(\ell,Q)=1\).

Since \(y\) is invertible modulo \(Q\), choose \(a\) such that
\[
ay\equiv x^k\pmod Q.
\]
By the Chinese remainder theorem, choose a residue class \(c\pmod{\ell Q}\) satisfying
\[
c\equiv a\pmod Q,\qquad c\equiv2\pmod\ell.
\]
This class is coprime to \(\ell Q\). Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions therefore gives a prime \(r\equiv c\pmod{\ell Q}\).

Then
\[
ry\equiv x^k\pmod Q,
\]
so
\[
(ry)^2\equiv x^{2k}\equiv-1\pmod Q.
\]
Thus \(Q\mid(ry)^2+1\). Applying the hypothesis with \(n=r\), where \(\varphi(r)=r-1\), yields
\[
Q\mid x^{r-1}-1.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(x)=4k\), we obtain \(4k\mid r-1\). As \(k=\ell L\), this implies \(\ell\mid r-1\). But \(r\equiv2\pmod\ell\), so \(r-1\equiv1\pmod\ell\), a contradiction.

Therefore \(x>1\) is impossible. Since \(x\) is a positive integer, \(x=1\).
outcome.stop_reason: The proof constructs a modulus coprime to \(xy\) on which \(x\) has exact order \(4\ell L\), then uses CRT and Dirichlet’s theorem to produce a prime forcing incompatible congruences modulo \(\ell\).
